The Illusion of the 90% in boards.

In today’s education system, students are constantly told that scoring 90% or above is the ultimate sign of intelligence and success. Schools, coaching institutes, and society often promote this idea so strongly that students begin to believe their entire worth depends on a number printed on a mark sheet.

But in reality, the 90% goal is largely an artificial benchmark.

It has gradually become a metric that many coaching classes and institutions use to advertise their results, boost their reputation, and attract more students. When a few students achieve high percentages, these results are showcased as proof of excellence, creating the illusion that marks alone define ability.

The Psychological Trap

Chasing a fixed number like 90% creates unnecessary psychological pressure on students.

Only a small percentage of students can realistically achieve such scores. As a result, many students develop:

Ego problems if they achieve the target

Inferiority complexes if they fall short

A constant feeling of incompleteness

These psychological burdens affect students far more deeply than a temporary exam result. A student who scores 88% may feel like a failure simply because the target was set at 90%. In reality, the difference between these numbers has almost no significance in the broader journey of life.

Marks are not useless, but they should be treated as feedback, not as a measure of a person’s intelligence or worth.
